 Retirees Who Pay Medicare Premiums and Prescriptions by Card Are Earning Rewards on Bills They Can’t Skip
 By Austin Smith 
 Published November 21, 2026, 1:58pm ET · 4 min read 
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Retirees can earn cash back on unavoidable health bills by putting fee-free payments on a rewards card and paying the balance in full monthly.
 Insurers set their own payment rules for Part D, Medicare Advantage and Medigap premiums, and convenience fees can wipe out the rewards.
 Part B only goes on a card if Medicare bills you; Social Security deductions leave nothing to charge, and Easy Pay earns no rewards.

 Some health bills arrive every month no matter what the market does. According to CMS, the standard Medicare Part B premium is $202.90 a month for 2026. CMS announced on November 17, 2026 [ 1 ] that it will rise to $209.40 in 2027. Add a Part D plan, a Medigap policy and pharmacy copays, and health care becomes one of the steadiest costs in a retirement budget. If you put the bills that take cards with no fee on a rewards card and pay it off in full, you earn cash back on money you were going to spend anyway.
 How much you earn depends on your card’s reward rate and the size of your bills. Higher-income retirees pay more. In 2026, the top total Part B premium is $689.90 a month for single filers with modified adjusted gross income over $500,000.
 Pharmacy Counter Purchases Are the Easiest Rewards to Capture
 You usually pay for prescription copays and over-the-counter items at the pharmacy counter, and pharmacies typically take cards, so check how your card issuer classifies pharmacy purchases, because the category it assigns determines which reward rate you get. Don’t buy extra items to chase rewards. The value comes from purchases already on your list.
 Private Plan Premiums Depend on Each Insurer’s Rules
 You pay Part D, Medicare Advantage and Medigap premiums to private insurance companies. CMS reports that roughly two-thirds of beneficiaries pay premiums directly to the plan instead of having them taken out of their Social Security checks. Each insurance companies determines which payment methods it accepts. Some take cards, some only take bank drafts and some charge a convenience fee, which can wipe out the rewards, so check your premium statement or call the insurance companies before you switch.
 The Part D income-related adjustment works differently. CMS says it is deducted from Social Security benefit checks or paid directly to Medicare, no matter how you pay your plan premium. In 2026 it runs from $14.50 to $91 a month for single filers above the income thresholds. That IRMAA surcharge is one of several add-ons linked to income from two years ago, and we mapped out the rest in a free Medicare guide .
 Part B Goes on a Card Only When Medicare Bills You
 According to Medicare.gov, most people have their Part B premium deducted automatically from their Social Security benefit [ 2 ] . If that’s how you pay, there is nothing to put on a card. People who don’t collect Social Security benefits get a bill instead, and that includes many retirees who sign up for Medicare but delay taking Social Security. A bill for Part B alone arrives every 3 months [ 2 ] .
 If you get a bill, Medicare.gov says you can pay by credit or debit card through your online Medicare account [ 2 ] . That option directs you to the Treasury’s Pay.gov site. You can also mail card details on the signed payment coupon. Medicare Easy Pay, the free automatic option, takes the money from a checking or savings account, so it earns no card rewards. Your premium bill or Medicare.gov lists the payment methods available to you.
 Pay the Full Balance Every Month or Rewards Lose
 The average credit card APR was 21.19% [ 3 ] as of August 2026. If you carry a balance, the interest will wipe out any rewards you earn. Set autopay to cover the full statement balance, and schedule it for after your Social Security deposit arrives so the cash is always there.
 Taxes are simple. Rewards earned on personal purchases are generally not treated as taxable income because they count as rebates on what you spent. That means they don’t raise the income figures Medicare uses to set premium surcharges.
 Who This Suits and What to Do First
 Retirees who already pay their card in full every month get the most from this, as do people charged directly for Part B, anyone who pays private plan premiums straight to the insurance companies and higher-income retirees whose surcharges make their bills bigger. If you tend to carry a balance, the interest will cost more than the rewards bring in.
 To start, list every health bill you pay: prescriptions, Part B, Part D, Medicare Advantage or Medigap. Next to each one, write how you pay it now and whether it takes cards without a fee. Move only the fee-free ones to your rewards card, then set up full-balance autopay before the next bill arrives.
